pos: n. (the Franconian abbey of 1127, the first Cistercian house east of the Rhine)
etymology: From German Eber, a boar, and Bach, a brook; the boar's stream.
biblical_def: Ebrach in the Steigerwald of Upper Franconia was founded in 1127 from Morimond and is the first Cistercian house east of the Rhine, the bridgehead from which the order crossed into Franconia, Bavaria, Bohemia and beyond. Its early Gothic church, consecrated in 1285, is one of the purest in Germany, and the rose window of its west front is famous; the conventual buildings were rebuilt in the eighteenth century with a grand staircase, and the whole complex has served as a prison since 1851. From Ebrach came Rein, Heilsbronn, Langheim and a long line of daughters. This dictionary records Ebrach for what a first house in a new country is. Scripture gives the pattern for a small beginning that is not despised, “who hath despised the day of small things?” (Zec 4:10), and the Lord's own figure for a work that starts smaller than it ends, “The kingdom of heaven is like to a grain of mustard seed” (Mat 13:31). The command to a people outgrowing its ground is to make room rather than to stop, “Enlarge the place of thy tent” (Isa 54:2), and the boundaries themselves are set by God, “hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation” (Act 17:26).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a colony as a company transplanted to a remote province; a frontier as the border of a country; to enlarge as to extend in limits; small as of little size; and a bound as a limit or boundary.
webster_full: COLONY, n. A company of people transplanted from their mother country to a remote province or country, and remaining subject to the jurisdiction of the parent state.
FRONTIER, n. The marches; the border, confine, or extreme part of a country, bordering on another country.
ENLARGE, v.t. To make greater in quantity or dimensions; to extend in limits, breadth or size; to expand.
SMALL, adj. Slender; thin; fine; of little size; minute; not great; little.
BOUND, n. A limit; the external or limiting line of any object or of space; hence, that which keeps in or restrains.
scriptures: Zec 4:10

For who hath despised the day of small things? for they shall rejoice, and shall see the plummet in the hand of Zerubbabel with those seven; they are the eyes of the LORD, which run to and fro through the whole earth.
Another parable put he forth unto them, saying, The kingdom of heaven is like to a grain of mustard seed, which a man took, and sowed in his field:
Isa 54:2
Enlarge the place of thy tent, and let them stretch forth the curtains of thine habitations: spare not, lengthen thy cords, and strengthen thy stakes;
And hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth, and hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation;
corruption_summary: Franconian abbey of 1127, the first Cistercian house east of the Rhine: a small beginning that carried the order into half of Europe.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God does not share our contempt for small beginnings. Twelve monks and an abbot in the Steigerwald became the head of a line of houses across central Europe, and the prophet rebukes in advance anyone who would have sneered at the first winter, “who hath despised the day of small things?” (Zec 4:10). The Lord chose the smallest seed on purpose, “is like to a grain of mustard seed” (Mat 13:31).

The second thing is that a frontier is not an accident. Ebrach stood where the order crossed into a new country, and Scripture insists that the placing of peoples and the drawing of their borders is God's own doing, “hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth” (Act 17:26). The answer to growth is enlargement rather than contentment with the tent one has, “spare not, lengthen thy cords, and strengthen thy stakes” (Isa 54:2).

pos: n. (the Franconian abbey of 1132, burial church of the Hohenzollern burgraves, turned Lutheran in 1533)
etymology: German Heil, salvation or healing, and Bronn, a spring; the well of salvation.
biblical_def: Heilsbronn in Middle Franconia was founded in 1132 by Bishop Otto of Bamberg and settled from Ebrach. Its name means the well of salvation, and the abbey became the burial church of the burgraves of Nuremberg and of the Hohenzollern margraves of Brandenburg-Ansbach, so that its minster holds a remarkable gallery of tombs. At the Reformation the margrave introduced Lutheran preaching; the last abbot resigned in 1578, the house was dissolved, and its endowments were turned into a Protestant school and seminary which trained ministers for two centuries. This dictionary records Heilsbronn for its name, which is a direct quotation of Scripture, and for what became of its revenues. The well of salvation is Isaiah's, “with joy shall ye draw water out of the wells of salvation” (Isa 12:3), and the Lord claims to be that water himself, “the water that I shall give him shall be in him a well of water springing up into everlasting life” (Joh 4:14). Jeremiah names the alternative and the folly of it, “they have forsaken me the fountain of living waters” (Jer 2:13), and the unstopping of old wells is itself a biblical act, “And Isaac digged again the wells of water, which they had digged in the days of Abraham” (Gen 26:18).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a well as a spring or fountain; salvation as deliverance from sin and its consequences; a fountain as a spring or source of water; to draw as to pull up water; and living as flowing, of water.
webster_full: WELL, n. A spring; a fountain; a pit or cylindrical hole sunk into the earth to such a depth as to reach a supply of water.
SALVATION, n. The redemption of man from the bondage of sin and liability to eternal death, and the conferring on him everlasting happiness.
FOUNTAIN, n. A spring, or source of water; the head or source of a stream; original; first principle or cause.
DRAW, v.t. To pull along; to haul; to take water from a well or a vessel; to derive; to deduce.
LIVING, adj. Having life; not dead; issuing continually, as living water; running, as a living spring.
scriptures: Isa 12:3
Therefore with joy shall ye draw water out of the wells of salvation.
Joh 4:14
But whosoever drinketh of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst; but the water that I shall give him shall be in him a well of water springing up into everlasting life.
Jer 2:13
For my people have committed two evils; they have forsaken me the fountain of living waters, and hewed them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water.

And Isaac digged again the wells of water, which they had digged in the days of Abraham his father; for the Philistines had stopped them after the death of Abraham: and he called their names after the names by which his father had called them.
corruption_summary: Franconian abbey of 1132, the well of salvation: Hohenzollern burial church, dissolved at the Reformation and turned into a school for preachers.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is in the name. A spring is something you come to and draw from, not something you manufacture, and that is exactly the figure Scripture chooses for salvation, “Therefore with joy shall ye draw water out of the wells of salvation” (Isa 12:3). The Lord then identifies the source as himself and makes the supply interior and permanent, “shall never thirst” (Joh 4:14).

The second thing is the end of the house. Its lands became a seminary that trained Lutheran ministers, which is a better use of a monastery than most dissolutions managed. Jeremiah's charge against his people was that they left the spring and dug substitutes, “they have forsaken me the fountain of living waters” (Jer 2:13); reopening a choked well is the opposite motion, and Isaac is commended for doing exactly that, “And Isaac digged again the wells of water” (Gen 26:18).

pos: n. (the Cistercian abbey of 1151 in the Tauber valley of Franconia)
etymology: German Bronn, a spring, and Bach, a brook; the stream from the spring.
biblical_def: Bronnbach lies in the Tauber valley of Franconia and was founded in 1151 from Maulbronn, with the church begun soon after and consecrated in 1222. It is a textbook of the transition from Romanesque to Gothic, built to the Cistercian plan with a flat east end and no tower, and the cloister, chapter house and Romanesque dormitory all survive; the baroque period added the abbot's apartments and the Joseph Hall. Secularised in 1803, it passed to the princes of Löwenstein and now belongs to the district. This dictionary records Bronnbach for its name and its water. The Cistercians chose valleys with streams because the Rule required them to live by their own labour, and a mill, a fishpond and a drain were theology as much as engineering. Scripture makes watered ground a figure of the blessed man, “like a tree planted by the rivers of water” (Psa 1:3), and promises water precisely where there is none, “I will make the wilderness a pool of water, and the dry land springs of water” (Isa 41:18). The turning of waste into standing water is God's own work, “He turneth the wilderness into a standing water” (Psa 107:35), and the desert is said to rejoice at it, “the desert shall rejoice, and blossom as the rose” (Isa 35:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a brook as a small natural stream; a valley as a hollow between hills; to irrigate as to water land; fruitful as producing abundantly; and a mill as a machine for grinding.
webster_full: BROOK, n. A small natural stream of water, or a current flowing from a spring or fountain, less than a river.
VALLEY, n. A hollow or low tract of land between hills or mountains; a vale.
IRRIGATE, v.t. To water; to wet; to moisten; to bedew; to water, as land, by causing a stream to flow upon it.
FRUITFUL, adj. Producing fruit in abundance; prolific; fertile; rich; bearing much.
MILL, n. A complicated engine or machine for grinding and reducing to fine particles grain, fruit or other substance.
scriptures: Psa 1:3
And he shall be like a tree planted by the rivers of water, that bringeth forth his fruit in his season; his leaf also shall not wither; and whatsoever he doeth shall prosper.
I will open rivers in high places, and fountains in the midst of the valleys: I will make the wilderness a pool of water, and the dry land springs of water.
He turneth the wilderness into a standing water, and dry ground into watersprings.
Isa 35:1
The wilderness and the solitary place shall be glad for them; and the desert shall rejoice, and blossom as the rose.
corruption_summary: Tauber-valley abbey of 1151: a house built where the water was, and a plain church that lets its proportions do the preaching.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that water in Scripture is never merely practical. The first psalm fixes the image of a life drawing on an unfailing supply, “like a tree planted by the rivers of water, that bringeth forth his fruit in his season” (Psa 1:3), and Isaiah applies it where supply is least likely, “I will open rivers in high places” (Isa 41:18). A valley with a stream in it was, to a Cistercian, a sermon he could live in.

The second is the plainness of the building. The order forbade towers and coloured glass, and at Bronnbach the result is a church that has nothing to say except its own proportions. The same restraint appears in Scripture's promises, which are extravagant about God's work and sober about ours, “He turneth the wilderness into a standing water, and dry ground into watersprings” (Psa 107:35), “The wilderness and the solitary place shall be glad for them” (Isa 35:1).

pos: n. (the Cistercian abbey of 1157 on the Jagst in Franconia, burial place of Götz von Berlichingen)
etymology: German schön, beautiful, and Tal, a valley; the fair valley.
biblical_def: Schöntal was founded about 1153 and settled in 1157 from Maulbronn, on the Jagst in what is now northern Württemberg. Its Romanesque cloister survives beneath an eighteenth-century rebuilding, and its baroque church by Leonhard Dientzenhofer, finished in 1736, is among the finest in the region. The abbey is best known to Germans as the burial place of Götz von Berlichingen, the iron-handed knight whose memoirs Goethe turned into a play, who died in 1562 and whose tomb slab is in the cloister. Secularised in 1802, the buildings now house a seminary and a school. This dictionary records Schöntal for the tombs in its cloister and the question they put. A monastery that buried knights sold them something, and Scripture is blunt about what survives a man. The name outlasts the estate, “A good name is rather to be chosen than great riches” (Pro 22:1), and the day of death is weighed against the day of birth, “A good name is better than precious ointment” (Ecc 7:1). What follows a man is his works rather than his monument, “and their works do follow them” (Rev 14:13), and the just are remembered without a slab, “the righteous shall be in everlasting remembrance” (Psa 112:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a tomb as a grave or vault for the dead; an epitaph as an inscription on a monument; a monument as something erected in memory; remembrance as the retaining of an idea in the mind; and fame as public report of character.
webster_full: TOMB, n. A grave; a pit in which the dead body of a human being is deposited; a house or vault, formed wholly or partly in the earth, for the reception of the dead.
EPITAPH, n. An inscription on a monument, in honor or memory of the dead.
MONUMENT, n. Any thing by which the memory of a person or of an event is preserved or perpetuated; a building, stone, or other thing placed or erected to remind men.
REMEMBRANCE, n. The retaining or having in mind the idea of a thing formerly known; recollection; honorable memory.
FAME, n. Public report or rumor; favorable report; report of good or great actions; renown.
scriptures: Pro 22:1
A good name is rather to be chosen than great riches, and loving favour rather than silver and gold.
Ecc 7:1
A good name is better than precious ointment; and the day of death than the day of one's birth.

And I heard a voice from heaven saying unto me, Write, Blessed are the dead which die in the Lord from henceforth: Yea, saith the Spirit, that they may rest from their labours; and their works do follow them.
Surely he shall not be moved for ever: the righteous shall be in everlasting remembrance.
corruption_summary: Fair-valley abbey of 1157 on the Jagst: a baroque church over a Romanesque cloister, and a knight's tomb that asks what survives a man.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Scripture's own measure of what lasts. A knight buried in a cloister has purchased a slab and a name; the Bible weighs the name itself rather than the stone, “A good name is rather to be chosen than great riches” (Pro 22:1), and makes the comparison as unflattering as possible, “and the day of death than the day of one's birth” (Ecc 7:1).

The live temptation the tombs represent is the hope of buying remembrance, which was precisely what a burial in a monastic church was sold as, with masses attached. Scripture gives no such market. What accompanies the dead is the work itself, “Blessed are the dead which die in the Lord” (Rev 14:13), and the memory of the righteous is secured by God rather than by masonry, “Surely he shall not be moved for ever” (Psa 112:6). The principle to recover is that a grave is a place to lie, not a transaction.

pos: n. (the Palatine Cistercian abbey of 1145, whose church was later shared by two confessions)
etymology: German Otter, an adder or otter, and Berg, a hill.
biblical_def: Otterberg in the Palatinate was founded in 1145 from Eberbach, and its abbey church, built between about 1168 and 1254, is the second largest church in the Palatinate after Speyer cathedral: a severe Cistercian hall whose west rose window is the finest in the region. The house was dissolved at the Reformation, the town was settled by Walloon and French refugees, and for nearly two centuries after 1707 the one church was divided by a wall and used by Lutherans at one end and by the Reformed at the other. The wall came down in 1979. This dictionary records Otterberg for that wall, because a building partitioned between two bodies of Protestants is a parable nobody intended. Scripture presses toward what builds rather than what divides, “follow after the things which make for peace, and things wherewith one may edify another” (Rom 14:19), and makes unity a thing to be laboured at, “Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Eph 4:3). The psalm that names the good of brethren together is short and unanswerable, “how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity” (Psa 133:1), and Christ prayed for exactly this, “That they all may be one” (Joh 17:21).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a partition as a division or separating wall; schism as a division in a church; to edify as to build up in faith; concord as agreement between persons; and communion as fellowship in a common faith.
webster_full: PARTITION, n. The act of dividing; division; separation; also, a wall which separates one apartment from another.
SCHISM, n. In a general sense, division or separation; but appropriately, a division or separation in a church or denomination of Christians.
EDIFY, v.t. To instruct and improve the mind in knowledge generally, and particularly in moral and religious knowledge, in faith and holiness.
CONCORD, n. Agreement between persons; union in opinions, sentiments, views or interests; peace; harmony.
COMMUNION, n. Fellowship; intercourse between two persons or more; interchange of transactions or offices; mutual intercourse or union in religious worship.
scriptures: Let us therefore follow after the things which make for peace, and things wherewith one may edify another.
Eph 4:3
Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.
A Song of degrees of David. Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!
That they all may be one; as thou, Father, art in me, and I in thee, that they also may be one in us: that the world may believe that thou hast sent me.
corruption_summary: Palatine abbey of 1145: the second largest church in the Palatinate, divided for two centuries by a wall between Lutheran and Reformed.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that division among believers is a wound rather than a tidy arrangement. Paul gives the test for any practice in dispute, and it is not who is more consistent but what builds, “Let us therefore follow after the things which make for peace” (Rom 14:19). Unity is treated as something already given by the Spirit and to be kept by effort, “Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit” (Eph 4:3).

This is not a plea to dissolve confessional differences, which are about truth and matter. It is an observation that two bodies of Protestants who agreed on nearly everything built a wall through one nave and left it for two hundred and seventy years. The psalm was on both sides of it, “how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity” (Psa 133:1), and so was the prayer of Christ, “That they all may be one; as thou, Father, art in me, and I in thee” (Joh 17:21). The principle to recover is that a wall should cost something to build.

pos: n. (the Westphalian Cistercian abbey of 1185, whose church survives as a parish church)
etymology: German Marien, of Mary, and Feld, a field; the field of Mary.
biblical_def: Marienfeld in Westphalia was founded in 1185 by a group of local nobles and settled from Hardehausen, and its church, consecrated in 1222, is a late Romanesque hall with early Gothic vaulting that still serves as the parish church of the village. The abbey was secularised in 1803 and most of its buildings sold or demolished, but the church, the gatehouse and the abbot's residence remain. Every Cistercian house carried the name of Mary, and this one wears it in its own name together with the word for a field. This dictionary records Marienfeld for that second word, because the field is one of Scripture's busiest images and the Cistercians worked more of them than anyone else in Europe. The Lord interprets the figure himself, “The field is the world; the good seed are the children of the kingdom” (Mat 13:38). Sowing is answered exactly, “whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap” (Gal 6:7), and the crop is nearer than it looks, “Lift up your eyes, and look on the fields; for they are white already to harvest” (Joh 4:35), while the shortage is never of work, “The harvest truly is plenteous, but the labourers are few” (Mat 9:37).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a field as a piece of land enclosed for tillage or pasture; to sow as to scatter seed; harvest as the season of gathering; a labourer as one who works with his hands; and tillage as the preparing of land for seed.
webster_full: FIELD, n. A piece of land enclosed for tillage or pasture; any part of the open country not covered with wood.
SOW, v.t. To scatter seed upon the ground for the purpose of growth; to spread abroad; to propagate.
HARVEST, n. The season of reaping and gathering in corn or other crops; the ripe corn or grain collected.
LABORER, n. One who labors in a toilsome occupation; a man who does work that requires little skill, as distinguished from an artisan.
TILLAGE, n. The operation, practice or art of tilling and preparing land for seed, and keeping the ground free from weeds.
scriptures: The field is the world; the good seed are the children of the kingdom; but the tares are the children of the wicked one;
Gal 6:7
Be not deceived; God is not mocked: for whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap.
Joh 4:35
Say not ye, There are yet four months, and then cometh harvest? behold, I say unto you, Lift up your eyes, and look on the fields; for they are white already to harvest.
Mat 9:37
Then saith he unto his disciples, The harvest truly is plenteous, but the labourers are few;
corruption_summary: Westphalian abbey of 1185, the field of Mary: an abbey church that outlived its abbey and still serves a parish.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the Lord's own reading of the figure. A field is not a metaphor for the church but for the world, with two crops growing in it together until the end, “The field is the world; the good seed are the children of the kingdom” (Mat 13:38). An order that cleared forest to plant grain was working a parable it did not always read carefully.

The second is the law of sowing, which Paul states without any softening and introduces with a warning against assuming an exception, “Be not deceived; God is not mocked” (Gal 6:7). Against that, the Lord's instruction is to look up rather than calculate, “Say not ye, There are yet four months, and then cometh harvest?” (Joh 4:35), and his complaint is never about the size of the crop, “The harvest truly is plenteous, but the labourers are few” (Mat 9:37). The field of Mary outlived the abbey because a parish kept working it.

pos: n. (the Westphalian house of 1196, Augustinian nuns turned Cistercian monks, later an ironworks)
etymology: From Middle Low German bred, broad, and l'ar, a clearing or pasture.
biblical_def: Bredelar in the Sauerland of Westphalia began about 1170 as a house of Augustinian canonesses and was handed over in 1196 to Cistercian monks from Hardehausen, who kept it until the secularisation of 1804. Its later history is unusual: the buildings were bought by an industrialist and turned into an ironworks and foundry, which ran there through the nineteenth century, so that the abbey church became a factory floor. It is now restored as a cultural centre. This dictionary records Bredelar because the iron that was smelted in its nave gives the entry its subject, and Scripture has more to say about iron than most readers expect. Job knows where it comes from, “Iron is taken out of the earth, and brass is molten out of the stone” (Job 28:2). Solomon makes a blunt edge an argument for wisdom rather than for effort, “If the iron be blunt, and he do not whet the edge, then must he put to more strength” (Ecc 10:10). Iron sharpens iron between men, “Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend” (Pro 27:17), and the prophets look for the day the metal is repurposed, “they shall beat their swords into plowshares” (Isa 2:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines iron as the most common and useful of metals; a forge as a furnace where iron is wrought; to temper as to bring to a proper degree of hardness; an edge as the thin cutting part of an instrument; and to whet as to sharpen by friction.
webster_full: IRON, n. A metal, the most common and most useful of all the metals, and the hardest and most elastic except steel.
FORGE, n. A furnace in which iron or other metal is heated and hammered into form; also, the work-place of a smith.
TEMPER, v.t. To bring to a proper degree of hardness; as, to temper iron or steel; to qualify by mixture.
EDGE, n. In a general sense, the extreme border or point of any thing; the sharp border; the thin cutting extremity of an instrument.
WHET, v.t. To rub for the purpose of sharpening; to sharpen by attrition; as, to whet a scythe or an ax.
scriptures: Job 28:2
Iron is taken out of the earth, and brass is molten out of the stone.
If the iron be blunt, and he do not whet the edge, then must he put to more strength: but wisdom is profitable to direct.
Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend.
Isa 2:4

And he shall judge among the nations, and shall rebuke many people: and they shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruninghooks: nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they learn war any more.
corruption_summary: Westphalian house of 1196: canonesses, then Cistercians, then an ironworks in the nave, and now a restored shell.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Solomon's, and it is about work rather than metal. A blunt tool is answered by most men with more effort; Scripture answers it with skill, “but wisdom is profitable to direct” (Ecc 10:10). A monastery that became a foundry and then a ruin and then a restored hall is a long argument for maintaining an edge.

The second is the sharpening that happens between people, which is the verse everybody knows and few submit to, “Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend” (Pro 27:17). Both pieces are hard, both lose metal, and the result is an edge neither had alone. The prophets end the matter by taking the same iron and changing its use entirely, “they shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruninghooks” (Isa 2:4).

Hebrew chokmah (H2451) — wisdom, profitable to direct; “but wisdom is profitable to direct”, Ecclesiastes 10:10.
Hebrew qalal (H7043) — to be blunted, made light; “If the iron be blunt, and he do not whet the edge”, Ecclesiastes 10:10.
Hebrew chadad (H2300) — to sharpen, iron on iron; “Iron sharpeneth iron”, Proverbs 27:17.
Hebrew 'eth (H855) — a plowshare, beaten from a sword; “they shall beat their swords into plowshares”, Isaiah 2:4.

“Iron sharpeneth iron” (Pro 27:17) — both pieces lose metal.
“they shall beat their swords into plowshares” (Isa 2:4) — the same iron, a new use.

pos: n. (the Bavarian Cistercian abbey founded in 1263 by Duke Ludwig II in penance for killing his wife on a false suspicion)
etymology: German Fürst, a prince, and Feld, a field; the prince's field.
biblical_def: Fürstenfeld, west of Munich, was founded in 1263 by Duke Ludwig II of Upper Bavaria as a penance. In 1256 he had his wife, Maria of Brabant, beheaded on a suspicion of adultery that rested on a misdelivered letter, discovered almost at once that the charge was false, and spent the rest of his life trying to pay for it; the abbey, settled from Aldersbach, was the largest instalment. Its baroque church, rebuilt from 1700, is one of the most sumptuous in Bavaria. The house was dissolved in 1803. This dictionary records Fürstenfeld because its origin is a textbook case of the sin Scripture legislates against most carefully. Judgment on one testimony is forbidden outright, “One witness shall not rise up against a man for any iniquity” (Deu 19:15), and answering before hearing is named folly, “He that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame unto him” (Pro 18:13). The first account always sounds right, “He that is first in his own cause seemeth just; but his neighbour cometh and searcheth him” (Pro 18:17), and the ninth commandment stands over the whole business, “Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbour” (Exo 20:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines penance as a punishment voluntarily undergone in token of repentance; a witness as one who testifies; to accuse as to charge with a crime; rash as uttered without due deliberation; and restitution as the act of restoring what was taken.
webster_full: PENANCE, n. The suffering, labor or pain to which a person voluntarily subjects himself, or which is imposed on him by authority as a punishment for his faults.
WITNESS, n. Testimony; attestation of a fact or event; that which furnishes evidence or proof; a person who knows or sees any thing.
ACCUSE, v.t. To charge with a crime, offense or fault, by a legal process; to blame or censure.
RASH, adj. Hasty in council or action; precipitate; resolving or entering on a project or measure without due deliberation.
RESTITUTION, n. The act of returning or restoring to a person some thing or right of which he has been unjustly deprived.
scriptures: One witness shall not rise up against a man for any iniquity, or for any sin, in any sin that he sinneth: at the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall the matter be established.
He that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame unto him.
He that is first in his own cause seemeth just; but his neighbour cometh and searcheth him.
Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbour.
corruption_summary: Bavarian abbey of 1263: founded by a duke who beheaded his wife on one letter and learned too late that the letter was misdelivered.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the hardest and most practical in the whole book of Proverbs. One account always sounds conclusive until the second arrives, “He that is first in his own cause seemeth just; but his neighbour cometh and searcheth him” (Pro 18:17), and acting before the second arrives is not decisiveness, “it is folly and shame unto him” (Pro 18:13). The law of Moses forbids conviction on a single witness precisely because a man in a hurry will believe one, “One witness shall not rise up against a man” (Deu 19:15).

The second thing is what penance cannot do. Ludwig built an abbey, endowed masses, and went on crusade, and Maria of Brabant remained dead. Scripture offers forgiveness freely to the guilty on confession, “I acknowledge my transgressions: and my sin is ever before me” (Psa 51:3), and it requires restitution where restitution is possible, “give again that he had robbed” (Eze 33:15). What it never offers is a payment that buys back an irreversible act. The principle to recover is to slow down before the blow, not after it.

Hebrew shama' (H8085) — to hear, before answering; “He that answereth a matter before he heareth it”, Proverbs 18:13.
Hebrew chaqar (H2713) — to search out, to examine a claim; “but his neighbour cometh and searcheth him”, Proverbs 18:17.
Hebrew sheqer (H8267) — falsehood, a lying testimony; “Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbour”, Exodus 20:16.
Hebrew yada' (H3045) — to acknowledge, to own a sin; “I acknowledge my transgressions”, Psalm 51:3.
usage: “He that is first in his own cause seemeth just” (Pro 18:17) — the misdelivered letter, stated in advance.
“One witness shall not rise up against a man” (Deu 19:15) — the law a duke ignored.
“it is folly and shame unto him” (Pro 18:13) — the verdict on a hasty verdict.

pos: n. (the Bavarian Cistercian abbey of 1146 on the Salzach, below Burghausen)
etymology: From Old High German hasal, hazel, with a personal name; the hazel wood of Raito.
biblical_def: Raitenhaslach stands on the Salzach below Burghausen and was founded in 1146 from Salem, the first Cistercian house in what is now Upper Bavaria. It grew rich on the salt trade of the river, holding salt rights at Reichenhall and shipping down the Salzach and the Inn, and it founded daughters at Fuerstenzell and elsewhere. The church was rebuilt in baroque between 1694 and 1739 with frescoes by Johann Zick; the abbey was dissolved in 1803 and the buildings now serve the Technical University of Munich. This dictionary records Raitenhaslach for the salt, which Scripture uses with unusual precision. Christ makes his people salt and then names the one failure that matters, “if the salt have lost his savour, wherewith shall it be salted?” (Mat 5:13). Speech is to be seasoned the same way, “Let your speech be alway with grace, seasoned with salt” (Col 4:6). Salt was required on every offering as a covenant sign, “neither shalt thou suffer the salt of the covenant of thy God to be lacking” (Lev 2:13), and a covenant of salt is the figure for one that does not spoil, “it is a covenant of salt for ever before the LORD” (Num 18:19).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines salt as a substance used for seasoning and preserving; savour as taste or odour; to season as to give a relish to; a covenant as a mutual agreement; and preservation as the act of keeping from decay.
webster_full: SALT, n. Common salt is the muriate of soda, a substance used for seasoning certain kinds of food, and for the preservation of meat.
SAVOR, n. Taste or odor; something that perceptibly affects the organs of taste or smell; relish; also, flavor.
SEASON, v.t. To render palatable, or to give a higher relish to, by the addition of salt, spices or condiments.
COVENANT, n. A mutual consent or agreement of two or more persons, to do or to forbear some act or thing; a contract; a stipulation.
PRESERVATION, n. The act of preserving or keeping safe; the act of keeping from injury, destruction or decay.
scriptures: Mat 5:13
Ye are the salt of the earth: but if the salt have lost his savour, wherewith shall it be salted? it is thenceforth good for nothing, but to be cast out, and to be trodden under foot of men.
Col 4:6
Let your speech be alway with grace, seasoned with salt, that ye may know how ye ought to answer every man.
Lev 2:13

And every oblation of thy meat offering shalt thou season with salt; neither shalt thou suffer the salt of the covenant of thy God to be lacking from thy meat offering: with all thine offerings thou shalt offer salt.

All the heave offerings of the holy things, which the children of Israel offer unto the LORD, have I given thee, and thy sons and thy daughters with thee, by a statute for ever: it is a covenant of salt for ever before the LORD unto thee and to thy seed with thee.
corruption_summary: Bavarian abbey of 1146 on the Salzach: the first Cistercian house in Upper Bavaria, grown rich on the salt trade of its own river.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that salt is defined by what it does to something else. It is useless in a heap and essential in a dish, which is exactly how Christ deploys the figure for his people, “Ye are the salt of the earth” (Mat 5:13), with the one failure named immediately, “if the salt have lost his savour” (Mat 5:13). A monastery that shipped salt down a river should have found the sermon easy.

The second use is covenantal and is easy to miss. Salt had to be on every offering, as a standing sign that the covenant would not spoil, “every oblation of thy meat offering shalt thou season with salt” (Lev 2:13), and the arrangement with the priests is described in the same terms, “it is a covenant of salt for ever before the LORD” (Num 18:19). Speech gets the same treatment, seasoned rather than bland or corrosive, “that ye may know how ye ought to answer every man” (Col 4:6).

“seasoned with salt” (Col 4:6) — speech neither bland nor corrosive.
“it is a covenant of salt for ever before the LORD” (Num 18:19) — a bond that does not spoil.

pos: n. (the Lower Bavarian abbey of Augustinian canons, Cistercian from 1146, now a brewery)
etymology: From Old High German elira, an alder, and Bach, a brook; the alder stream.
biblical_def: Aldersbach in Lower Bavaria was founded about 1120 as a house of Augustinian canons and was handed to the Cistercians in 1146, settled from Ebrach. It founded Raitenhaslach's neighbours and Gotteszell, and prospered on farming and on the brewery it ran from the fifteenth century. The church was remodelled from 1718 by the Asam brothers, whose stucco and frescoes make it one of the great rococo interiors of Bavaria. The abbey was dissolved in 1803; the brewery passed to private hands and is still working, so that the name survives on a bottle rather than a breviary. This dictionary records Aldersbach for that survival, and for what Scripture actually says about strong drink, which is neither of the two things people expect. It is given for gladness, “wine that maketh glad the heart of man” (Psa 104:15), and it is dangerous in exactly the way a deceiver is, “Wine is a mocker, strong drink is raging” (Pro 20:1). Drunkenness is forbidden and contrasted with the Spirit, “be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit” (Eph 5:18), and a little is prescribed as medicine, “use a little wine for thy stomach's sake” (1Ti 5:23).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a brewery as a house where beer is made; malt as grain steeped and dried; wine as the fermented juice of grapes; temperance as moderation in the indulgence of appetite; and drunkenness as intoxication.
webster_full: BREWERY, n. A brewhouse; the house and apparatus where brewing is carried on.
MALT, n. Barley or other grain steeped in water until it germinates, then dried in a kiln, used in brewing.
WINE, n. The fermented juice of grapes; also, the juice of certain fruits, prepared with sugar and spirits.
TEMPERANCE, n. Moderation; particularly, habitual moderation in regard to the indulgence of the natural appetites and passions.
DRUNKENNESS, n. Intoxication; inebriation; a state in which a person is overwhelmed or overpowered with spirituous liquors.
scriptures: And wine that maketh glad the heart of man, and oil to make his face to shine, and bread which strengtheneth man's heart.
Pro 20:1
Wine is a mocker, strong drink is raging: and whosoever is deceived thereby is not wise.
Eph 5:18
And be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit;
Drink no longer water, but use a little wine for thy stomach's sake and thine often infirmities.
corruption_summary: Lower Bavarian abbey, Cistercian from 1146: an Asam rococo church, and a brewery that outlived the house and still carries its name.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Scripture holds two things about wine at once and will not let either go. It is a gift with a stated purpose, “wine that maketh glad the heart of man” (Psa 104:15), and it is personified as a mocker that makes fools of the men who trust it, “Wine is a mocker, strong drink is raging: and whosoever is deceived thereby is not wise” (Pro 20:1). Prohibition and licence both solve the tension by dropping half the testimony.

The live error at a monastery brewery is not the brewing but the excess, and Paul puts the prohibition beside its true alternative rather than beside abstinence, “be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit” (Eph 5:18). He also, in the same letter-writing hand, prescribes a little for a sick man's stomach, “use a little wine for thy stomach's sake and thine often infirmities” (1Ti 5:23). A dictionary that will quote one of these verses should be willing to quote all four.

Greek asotia (G810) — riot, unsavedness, excess; “be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess”, Ephesians 5:18.
Greek astheneia (G769) — infirmity, a bodily weakness; “and thine often infirmities”, 1 Timothy 5:23.
usage: “wine that maketh glad the heart of man” (Psa 104:15) — a stated purpose, not a concession.
“Wine is a mocker, strong drink is raging” (Pro 20:1) — the same substance, personified as a liar.
“but be filled with the Spirit” (Eph 5:18) — the alternative Paul actually names.
